steps.thought: The handover note says what was run and, more usefully, what was not: no prune, no clone, no fetch. That is the difference between a recovery and an apology.
steps.tool_output:
# Handover note

`repo/` is the feedloader checkout. `feature` was three commits of Priya's work on the
vendor's rate limiting, branched off `main` before the CRLF change landed on it.

I rebased it onto `main` this morning and deleted a line out of the todo list by mistake.
The branch came back with two commits on it instead of three. The one in the middle, the
backoff work, is not on the branch any more.

Then I made it worse. While tidying up I ran

    git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all

so the reflog no longer has the entry for where `feature` used to point. What I have not
done is run a garbage collection, and I have not cloned, pushed or fetched anything since,
so whatever is left of that commit is still inside `repo/.git`. There is one copy of it.
Please read before you write.

There is no remote, no stash and no second checkout. Priya is out until Thursday, and the
commit is not on her machine either: she pushed it to this checkout and deleted her branch.

What I need back: `feature` with its three commits, in the order they were written, sitting
on top of `main` where the rebase was trying to put them. Priya's commit has to still be
her commit, with the same content, the same message, her name and her date on it. `main`
has not moved and should not.

steps.thought: fsck walks the object database instead of the refs, which is the only thing left that can see an object nothing points at. One dangling commit, which will be the tip feature had before the rebase: the dropped commit is not dangling itself because that tip still references it.

Put a ref on it before doing anything else. Until something points at that commit it is one garbage collection away from gone, and the next few commands are exactly the sort that make git think about running one. Naming it first costs nothing and makes the rest of this reversible.

tool_args.command:
lost=$(git -C repo fsck --dangling --no-progress | awk '/dangling commit/{print $3; exit}')
git -C repo branch rescue "$lost"
git -C repo log --oneline --decorate rescue | head

steps.thought: Move feature back to where it was before the rebase. -B resets the branch and checks it out in one go, which avoids a detached HEAD, and the tree is clean so nothing is at risk. tool_args.summary: The dropped commit was still in the object database with nothing pointing at it, and the reflog that would normally have found it had been expired. git fsck --dangling reported the pre rebase tip of feature; the two missing commits hang off it. Named that commit with a temporary branch first so nothing could prune it, confirmed it was Priya's three commits, moved feature back onto it with checkout -B, and reran the rebase onto main without deleting anything from the todo list. feature is now three commits above main in the original order, the recovered commit has its original tree, message, author and author date, main never moved, and the temporary ref is gone.
